title: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
summary: The attacks, far from the front lines, forced the only bridge between Russia and the occupied Crimean Peninsula to close. Traffic on two bridges in Kyiv was also stopped.

The only bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula was temporarily closed on Tuesday morning after suffering damage from a series of Ukrainian attacks, according to Russian officials.


Overnight, two of the main bridges over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital, were also temporarily closed after Russian strikes on the structures late on Monday, Ukrainian officials said.


The dual strikes on important bridges hundreds of miles from the front lines were part of a long-running battle in Russia’s war against Ukraine, involving logistics, symbols and survival. Bridges are some of the hardest structures to bring down using long-range weapons and such structures have repeatedly defied quick destruction.


The extent of the damage to the Ukrainian and Russian bridges was not immediately clear as engineering teams on both sides were dispatched to assess the aftermath of the attacks.


The Kerch Strait Bridge between Russia and Crimea,[a 12-mile span](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2022/10/08/world/russia-ukraine-war-news/a-fireball-erupts-on-a-bridge-linking-crimea-to-russia?smid=url-share) that holds both military and political significance for the Kremlin, suffered structural damage, according to Russia’s Investigative Committee, the country’s equivalent of the F.B.I.


The Russian Transport Ministry said in a statement that road and rail traffic on the bridge had been suspended while inspections were conducted.


“Motorists are advised not to travel toward the Crimean Bridge and to monitor the operational situation in official sources,” the ministry said.


Russia[illegally annexed Crimea](https://www.nytimes.com/2014/03/19/world/europe/ukraine.html) from Ukraine in 2014, and Kyiv has repeatedly attacked the Kerch Strait Bridge since[Russia’s full-scale invasion](https://www.nytimes.com/news-event/ukraine-russia) in 2022. Ukrainian forces have tried, unsuccessfully, to take the bridge down in unconventional sabotage operations and by direct bombardments.


In October 2022, a[truck bombing](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/10/08/world/europe/ukraine-crimea-bridge-explosion.html) collapsed sections of the bridge and ignited a passing fuel train. Ukrainian forces followed up with[a naval drone strike](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/07/17/world/europe/crimea-bridge-attack-russia-ukraine.html) in July 2023 that damaged the road deck. In June 2025, Ukraine carried out[an underwater demolition operation](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/06/03/world/europe/russia-ukraine-crimea-bridge.html) in which operatives detonated more than a metric ton of explosives against the bridge’s submerged support pillars.


Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Tuesday that the capital’s Northern and Southern bridges were closed to traffic after the Russian missile attack Monday night.


“We will provide updates as soon as new information becomes available. Municipal services are working on the ground,” Mr. Klitschko[said in a statement](https://t.me/vitaliy_klitschko/8153) . “We are doing everything possible to restore traffic as quickly as possible.”


Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.
